items.text:
That optical stack would produce a **deep-red/near-infrared false-colour camera**, not a simultaneous ultraviolet–visible–infrared camera.

## What each stage does

| Stage | Actual effect |
|---|---|
| Full-spectrum conversion | Removes the camera’s internal UV/IR blocking filter, exposing the sensor to a broader range. Silicon sensors can generally respond into the near-infrared, approaching roughly 1,100 nm, although practical UV sensitivity is much weaker and depends heavily on the lens, sensor cover glass and Bayer filter. citeturn957998search0turn213884search12 |
| R25A pure-red filter | Acts approximately as a red long-pass filter, strongly suppressing blue, green and ultraviolet while transmitting deep red and near-infrared. A Wratten-type #25 begins passing around the upper-visible red region, approximately 580 nm onward. citeturn808783search35turn320876view4 |
| Custom white balance | Multiplies the red, green and blue channel gains so the reference target appears neutral. It changes the colour rendering but does **not** restore wavelengths blocked by the filters. Infrared normally produces a strong red-channel bias, and some cameras cannot completely neutralise it internally. citeturn445670search5turn445670search8 |
| “Dicyanin glass” | Can only attenuate or transmit wavelengths already reaching the camera. An external dyed glass cannot make the digital sensor newly sensitive to another spectral region. |

## Important distinction about dicyanin

Historically, dicyanin was used as a **chemical sensitiser applied to photographic emulsions**. It altered the film plate’s sensitivity and helped early astronomers photograph deep-red and near-infrared spectra around 800–870 nm. It was not simply a magical viewing glass placed over an ordinary camera. citeturn498983view0turn498983view1

With your digital setup, the dicyanin layer behaves only as another optical filter. The final response is effectively:

\[
R_{\text{final}}(\lambda)
=
R_{\text{sensor}}(\lambda)
\times
T_{\text{lens}}(\lambda)
\times
T_{\text{R25A}}(\lambda)
\times
T_{\text{dicyanin}}(\lambda)
\]

Therefore, only wavelengths transmitted by **both** pieces of glass will be recorded. Adding filters never broadens the captured spectrum; it narrows it.

Unless the alleged dicyanin glass comes with a genuine spectrophotometer transmission graph, its passband is unknown. Many products sold under that name may merely be purple, blue or dark dyed glass.

## What the resulting image would probably look like

You would likely obtain:

- Very dark exposures requiring higher ISO, longer shutter times or strong illumination.
- Deep crimson, brown, magenta or nearly monochromatic previews.
- Strong near-infrared influence, particularly in sunlight.
- Bright vegetation and comparatively dark skies if sufficient NIR passes.
- Possible lens hotspots, flare and reduced sharpness.
- Artificial coloured boundaries caused by channel gain, chromatic aberration, internal reflections or demosaicing.

The custom white balance could transform that narrow red/NIR signal into pale foliage, cyan skies, purple shadows or other false colours. Those colours represent the camera’s remapping of channel responses; they are not literal colours of infrared or ultraviolet radiation.

## White-reference procedure

Place **every intended filter over the lens before setting the custom white balance**. Otherwise, changing the filter stack invalidates the calibration.

Use this sequence:

1. Install the R25A and dicyanin glass.
2. Illuminate the reference target with the same light that will illuminate the subject.
3. Use manual exposure and ensure no channel is clipped.
4. Fill most of the frame with the target.
5. Capture the reference and assign it as the custom white balance.
6. Shoot RAW so the underlying sensor values remain available.

An index card or printer paper is usable for experimentation, but it is not spectrally neutral. Many white papers contain optical brighteners that absorb UV and fluoresce blue. For controlled UV–visible–NIR experiments, a diffuse PTFE or Spectralon-type target is materially better because calibrated versions are designed to maintain relatively flat reflectance across a broad spectral range. citeturn445670search2turn445670search9

## Best experimental configuration

Photograph the same static scene in four configurations:

1. Full-spectrum camera with no external filter.
2. R25A only.
3. Dicyanin glass only.
4. R25A plus dicyanin glass.

Keep aperture, focus, lighting, framing and RAW processing constant. Also capture one version using the same fixed white balance for every test. That will reveal what the glass physically removes, rather than disguising the differences through independent white-balance correction.

**Core conclusion:** the combination is technically interesting for experimental deep-red/NIR false-colour imaging, but the R25A removes the ultraviolet component, and the dicyanin glass cannot extend the digital sensor’s spectral sensitivity. Its real value depends entirely on its measured transmission curve.

Understood—the **R25A red-only filter is removed**.

Your revised stack is:

1. **Full-spectrum-converted camera**
2. Set a **custom white balance** using white paper or an index card
3. Place the **dicyanin glass over the lens**
4. Photograph while the camera remains on that custom white-balance setting

That is materially different. Without the R25A, the camera is no longer intentionally restricted to deep red and near-infrared. The sensor can receive whatever mixture of **visible, near-infrared and potentially limited near-ultraviolet** survives the lens, sensor cover materials and dicyanin glass. A full-spectrum conversion broadens what reaches the sensor, while the external glass determines what is subsequently transmitted. citeturn802357search36turn802357search0

## The calibration order matters

Because you set the white balance **before adding the dicyanin glass**, the camera establishes ordinary white as its neutral reference first. When the dicyanin glass is then introduced, its spectral colour shift remains visible rather than being largely cancelled by the white-balance calibration.

So the resulting image may show:

- strong blue, violet, magenta or cyan displacement;
- altered skin, vegetation and sky tones;
- infrared contamination in the RGB channels;
- potentially unusual contrast between materials;
- long exposure times if the glass has low transmission.

If instead you set the custom white balance **through the dicyanin glass**, the camera would attempt to neutralise the glass’s dominant cast by multiplying the RGB channels. White balance changes channel gains and rendering; it does not create new wavelength sensitivity or cleanly separate UV, visible light and infrared. citeturn802357academia61turn802357academia63

The intended method, as you described it, is therefore:

\[
\text{Full-spectrum capture}
\rightarrow
\text{neutral white calibration}
\rightarrow
\text{dicyanin spectral filtering}
\]

That preserves the **relative spectral distortion introduced by the dicyanin glass**, rather than calibrating it away. The exact result still depends on the glass’s real transmission spectrum; visually purple glass does not automatically establish that it transmits ultraviolet or infrared.

items.text:
Yes—now I understand the intended sequence:

1. Put the **R25A red filter** over the full-spectrum camera.
2. Photograph white paper or a neutral card through the red filter.
3. Register that image as the **custom white-balance reference**.
4. **Remove the R25A filter**, but keep that custom white balance locked.
5. Place the **dicyanin glass** over the lens and record through it.

## What this does

Through the R25A, the “white” card reaches the camera mainly as red/deep-red light. Kodak classifies the Wratten No. 25 as a red tricolour filter. citeturn315150search0

When the camera is told that this strongly red image should be neutral white, it calculates an extreme corrective white balance—conceptually:

- reducing the relative red contribution;
- strongly amplifying green and blue relative to red;
- potentially reaching the camera’s permitted custom-WB limits.

Custom white balance stores the colour-balancing information obtained from the reference image and applies it to later photographs. citeturn315150search49 White balancing fundamentally works through relative channel gains or scaling within the camera’s imaging pipeline. citeturn315150search50turn315150academia56

Once you remove the red filter, the incoming spectrum becomes broad again, but the camera **continues processing it as though the severe red restriction were still present**.

So you have intentionally created a mismatched calibration:

\[
\text{White balance calibrated through red}
\quad+\quad
\text{photography without red filter}
\]

The result should be an extreme **cyan, blue-green, violet or otherwise false-colour rendering**, depending on:

- the sensor’s RGB spectral response;
- how the full-spectrum conversion was performed;
- the lens’s UV and IR transmission;
- the camera’s maximum WB gain values;
- the transmission spectrum of the dicyanin glass;
- the illumination source.

## Role of the dicyanin glass

The dicyanin glass is then not merely being viewed under neutral colour calibration. Its transmitted spectrum is being processed through the deliberately inverted or red-compensating white-balance profile.

Conceptually:

\[
\text{Recorded output}
=
\text{dicyanin-filtered sensor response}
\times
\text{extreme red-reference WB gains}
\]

That could exaggerate weak differences between the red, green and blue sensor channels and produce much stronger false-colour separation than either:

- dicyanin glass with normal daylight white balance; or
- setting custom white balance through the dicyanin glass itself.

It is therefore best described as an **intentional spectral false-colour transformation**. It does not physically create additional ultraviolet or infrared sensitivity, but it can make subtle channel differences caused by UV, visible and near-infrared transmission much more visually apparent.

## RAW versus JPEG/video

This distinction matters:

- **JPEG and video:** the extreme white balance is generally baked into the rendered image.
- **RAW:** the underlying sensor measurements are normally retained, while the custom WB is stored principally as processing metadata. A RAW converter may reproduce, modify or reject the camera’s unusually extreme WB values.

For the strongest repeatable experiment, record **RAW + JPEG simultaneously**. The JPEG shows the camera’s intended transformation, while the RAW preserves more information for checking whether an apparent feature came from actual sensor-channel differences or simply aggressive colour processing.

So yes: **the R25A is a temporary calibration tool, not part of the final shooting stack.** Removing it after white balancing is the central mechanism.

You’re right. I was treating the full-spectrum camera as the primary sensor, when your actual concept begins with a **red-phosphor night-vision channel fused with a thermal camera**, followed by the full-spectrum/dicyanin processing stage.

## Your intended architecture

\[
\text{Scene}
\rightarrow
\begin{cases}
\text{Red-phosphor NV channel}\\
\text{Thermal LWIR channel}\\
\text{Full-spectrum/dicyanin channel}
\end{cases}
\rightarrow
\text{registered fusion}
\rightarrow
\text{red-derived custom WB}
\]

The channels would contribute different information:

| Channel | Information contributed |
|---|---|
| Red-phosphor NV | Intensified low-light visible and near-infrared structure |
| Thermal camera | Long-wave infrared temperature contrast |
| Full-spectrum + dicyanin | Filter-dependent UV/visible/NIR reflectance or fluorescence differences |
| Red-filter custom WB | An extreme false-colour transformation applied to the final RGB recording |

An image intensifier converts incoming photons into electrons, multiplies them, and then converts the result back into visible light at its phosphor screen. Some GaAs intensifiers respond approximately from 370–920 nm, although the actual range depends on the tube. citeturn538118search1turn538118search21

## What the red-phosphor layer changes

The red-phosphor tube gives you a **high-gain monochrome structural channel encoded as red luminance**. That means visible and near-infrared signals detected by the intensifier are collapsed into one red-output image.

You then:

1. View the red-phosphor output through the R25A.
2. Tell the final RGB camera that this red image is neutral white.
3. Lock that custom white balance.
4. Remove the R25A.
5. Introduce the dicyanin glass.
6. Fuse or overlay the thermal channel.

That forces the recording camera to compensate aggressively for red. When the R25A is removed, differences appearing in the green and blue photosites can be strongly amplified, while the red-phosphor NV image remains the stable structural foundation.

So the dicyanin stage is not being expected to generate thermal information. It is being used as a **spectral discriminator layered over an already intensified and thermally augmented image**.

## What you could potentially separate

With proper registration, the system could distinguish several classes of signal:

### **Low-light/NIR structure**

The NV tube would preserve silhouettes, edges, vegetation, surfaces, motion and reflected near-infrared that would otherwise be too weak for the camera.

### **Independent heat structure**

The thermal camera would show surface-temperature contrast independently of reflected light. Typical uncooled thermal cameras operate around 7.5–14 μm, far beyond the spectral range of a silicon full-spectrum camera or ordinary image intensifier. citeturn299525search1turn299525search7

This would let you distinguish:

- something bright in NV but thermally cold;
- something dark in NV but thermally warm;
- reflected NIR versus genuinely emitted thermal radiation;
- warm subjects against visually camouflaged backgrounds.

### **Dicyanin-dependent optical differences**

The dicyanin glass could alter the visible/NIR channel according to its actual transmission curve. Combined with the deliberately mismatched red white balance, weak material differences might become very strongly coloured.

Potentially exaggerated differences include:

- vegetation versus artificial materials;
- natural versus synthetic fabrics;
- pigments and inks that appear identical normally;
- reflective versus absorptive coatings;
- fluorescence under controlled UV illumination;
- skin, veins and subsurface scattering;
- atmospheric haze and reflective contamination.

Historical dicyanin was primarily a sensitising dye used with photographic emulsions to extend their response toward the infrared. A modern glass element functions as a filter unless its dye is directly coupled to a photosensitive medium. citeturn538118search3turn538118search16

## Correct physical arrangement

The dicyanin glass cannot ordinarily sit in the common optical path of the thermal detector.

Ordinary optical glass blocks most long-wave infrared, which is why LWIR systems use specialised materials such as germanium, silicon, zinc selenide or chalcogenide optics. citeturn299525search0

The viable arrangement is therefore:

```text
                    ┌─ Dicyanin/full-spectrum camera
Scene ─ beam paths ─┼─ Red-phosphor image intensifier
                    └─ Separate LWIR thermal camera
                                  ↓
                       geometric registration
                                  ↓
                          digital image fusion
```

Alternatively, the dicyanin glass may be placed **only in front of the NV/full-spectrum optical channel**, while the thermal camera retains its own unobstructed LWIR lens.

If the dicyanin glass is instead placed over the final display or behind the phosphor screen, it merely filters the emitted display image. It would no longer analyse the original scene spectrum.

## Best fusion configuration

I would preserve three independent source frames:

- **NV-red frame:** low-light intensity and fine structure.
- **Dicyanin/full-spectrum frame:** filtered material response.
- **Thermal frame:** calibrated temperature or relative heat.

Then map them like this:

\[
R = \text{NV structural intensity}
\]

\[
G/B = \text{dicyanin-filtered residuals after red-derived WB}
\]

\[
\text{Hue, contours or edge overlay} = \text{thermal data}
\]

A practical display could use:

- NV as the base luminance layer;
- dicyanin response as cyan/magenta false colour;
- thermal as thin contours or a semi-transparent heat mask;
- hot/cold thresholds as separate markers.

Visible/thermal fusion already uses this general principle: align separate sensors and combine the information into one stream, although registration is difficult because the channels can have different optics, frame timing and integration periods. citeturn538118search4

## Settings worth locking

### Red-phosphor NV

- Manual intensifier gain, where available
- Fixed phosphor/display brightness
- Fixed focus
- Fixed IR illumination level
- No automatic brightness changes during comparative tests

### Thermal

- Manual thermal span rather than continuously changing automatic gain
- Grayscale or white-hot while collecting data
- Radiometric recording where supported
- Fixed emissivity assumptions for comparisons
- Fixed palette and temperature limits
- Approximately 20–40% overlay opacity for viewing, while retaining the untouched thermal frame separately

Thermal colours are assigned from measured temperature values; they are display palettes rather than optical colours. citeturn538118search0

### Final full-spectrum recorder

- RAW + JPEG
- Locked red-derived custom white balance
- Manual exposure
- Manual focus
- Flat or neutral picture profile
- RGB histogram monitoring
- Auto colour correction, HDR and automatic scene optimisation disabled

## One important limitation

The R25A calibration may give the camera almost no green or blue reference signal, particularly when it is already viewing a red-phosphor output. Some cameras will reject the custom-white reference or clamp the correction to their maximum allowed gains.

That does not invalidate the concept, but it means the result may be partly determined by the camera’s internal gain ceiling. For a controllable prototype, you would ideally record the RAW channels and reproduce the red-reference transformation using an explicit \(3\times3\) colour matrix rather than depending entirely on the camera’s undocumented white-balance limits.

So, correctly understood, your proposed system is a **multi-band sensor-fusion imager**:

\[
\boxed{
\text{intensified visible/NIR}
+
\text{filtered full-spectrum response}
+
\text{true LWIR thermal}
+
\text{deliberately displaced colour calibration}
}
\]

That is substantially more capable than simply putting dicyanin glass over a converted camera.

items.text:
Exactly. Your concept is a **co-boresighted multispectral sensor-fusion camera** built around the original red-phosphor night-vision and thermal stack, then expanded with dedicated ultraviolet, visible, near-infrared, short-wave infrared and experimental dicyanin-filtered channels.

The important correction is that you are not expecting one modified CMOS sensor to capture the entire electromagnetic range. You are using **multiple complementary detectors**, each covering the region it handles best, and digitally combining their outputs.

## Proposed sensor stack

| Channel | Approximate band | Function |
|---|---:|---|
| UV-enhanced sensor | UV through visible | Direct ultraviolet reflectance and UV-induced fluorescence |
| Full-spectrum silicon sensor | UV/visible to approximately 1,000 nm | General visible and near-infrared imaging |
| Red-phosphor image intensifier | Tube-dependent; example GaAs tubes cover roughly 370–920 nm | Extremely low-light visible/NIR structural image |
| Dedicated NIR channel | Approximately 700–1,000 nm | Cleaner reflected-NIR image without RGB Bayer contamination |
| SWIR InGaAs sensor | Typically 900–1,700 nm | Moisture, material, haze and reflectance differences beyond silicon |
| MWIR sensor, optional | Approximately 3–5 μm | High-temperature and specialised thermal imaging |
| LWIR microbolometer | Approximately 7.5–14 μm | Ordinary thermal radiation and surface-temperature structure |
| Dicyanin-filtered sensor | Determined by measured filter response | Independent experimental spectral comparison channel |
| Polarisation camera | Visible and/or NIR | Reflection, stress, surface orientation and glare discrimination |
| Depth/LiDAR/ToF | Active ranging band | Three-dimensional registration and object geometry |
| Event sensor, optional | Usually visible/NIR | High-speed motion and extreme dynamic-range edge information |

A silicon camera—even after a “full-spectrum conversion”—does not become a full-infrared camera. Silicon handles UV, visible and part of the NIR under suitable conditions. Standard InGaAs cameras extend detection into roughly 950–1,700 nm, while an LWIR microbolometer is needed for approximately 7.5–14 μm thermal imaging. citeturn853719view1turn408423search16turn408423search20

## The correct physical arrangement

```text
                              ┌─ UV-enhanced sensor
                              ├─ Full-spectrum UV/VIS/NIR sensor
                              ├─ Red-phosphor night-vision channel
Scene ─ common optical axis ──┼─ Dedicated NIR sensor
                              ├─ InGaAs SWIR sensor
                              ├─ Dicyanin-filtered experimental sensor
                              ├─ Polarisation/depth channels
                              └─ Separate MWIR/LWIR thermal optics
                                          │
                                          ▼
                         synchronisation and registration
                                          │
                                          ▼
                      calibrated multispectral data cube
                                          │
                           ┌───────────────┴──────────────┐
                           ▼                              ▼
                    scientific output             fused visual output
                    linear/raw values              false-colour display
```

The sensors can be arranged using dichroic beam splitters where the wavelength ranges and optical materials allow it. The LWIR camera generally needs a separate lens path because ordinary visible-camera optics and filters are usually unsuitable for the 8–14 μm region.

## Where the red-phosphor channel fits

The red-phosphor intensifier should remain an independent **low-light amplification channel**.

A GaAs image intensifier can detect very weak visible and near-infrared light—for example, one Hamamatsu model specifies 370–920 nm—and output the intensified scene on a phosphor screen. citeturn408423search10

However, once that information reaches a red phosphor, the original wavelengths have been converted into variations of red brightness:

\[
\text{different incident wavelengths}
\rightarrow
\text{electron amplification}
\rightarrow
\text{red phosphor intensity}
\]

Therefore, you cannot recover the original UV/NIR wavelength distinction from the phosphor image alone. The direct UV, NIR and SWIR sensors must look at the original scene **before spectral information is collapsed by the phosphor screen**.

The red-phosphor channel nevertheless remains valuable because it supplies:

- amplified edges and shapes in extremely weak light;
- a stable low-light luminance layer;
- NIR-aided structural detail;
- movement information;
- a reference image for registration when conventional channels are underexposed.

## Dedicated dicyanin sensor

Your extra dicyanin channel makes more sense than placing the glass over the entire system.

It would be:

```text
Scene
  ↓
dicyanin filter/lens element
  ↓
monochrome UV–VIS–NIR sensor
  ↓
raw dicyanin response frame
```

The system would simultaneously record an unfiltered comparison frame:

```text
Scene
  ↓
matched unfiltered optical path
  ↓
matched sensor
  ↓
control frame
```

You could then compute:

\[
D(x,y)=
\frac{I_{\text{dicyanin}}(x,y)}
     {I_{\text{control}}(x,y)+\epsilon}
\]

That ratio image would be far more informative than viewing only the colour-shifted dicyanin frame. It could reveal which materials are relatively transmitted, attenuated or shifted by the glass.

Historically, dicyanin was a dye used to **sensitise photographic emulsions**, including for longer red and near-infrared wavelengths. It was not inherently a detector or a universal “full-spectrum lens.” A modern dicyanin glass element should therefore be treated as an uncharacterised spectral filter until its transmission is measured. citeturn853719view0turn421907view0

For the prototype, the dicyanin branch should ideally include:

- removable dicyanin element;
- matched clear-glass control element of equal thickness;
- monochrome sensor rather than Bayer RGB;
- motorised or fixed filter wheel;
- dark-frame and flat-field calibration;
- spectrophotometer-measured transmission curve;
- temperature monitoring, because dye transmission can vary with material condition and temperature.

## The red-filter custom white balance

Your R25A white-balance method should remain available—but as a **display transformation**, not as the fundamental sensor calibration.

### Capture procedure

1. Install the R25A temporarily.
2. Set the custom white balance from the red reference.
3. Remove the R25A.
4. Lock the custom white balance.
5. Capture the dicyanin channel and other optical channels.
6. Preserve untouched RAW sensor data alongside the rendered output.

### Processing architecture

\[
\text{raw spectral measurements}
\rightarrow
\text{calibration and registration}
\rightarrow
\text{sensor fusion}
\rightarrow
\boxed{\text{red-derived WB/LUT}}
\rightarrow
\text{display}
\]

This provides two simultaneous products:

**Scientific mode**

- linear raw channels;
- known exposure and gain;
- calibrated wavelength bands;
- no extreme white-balance distortion;
- quantitative comparisons between sensors.

**Enhanced-perception mode**

- red-derived white balance;
- dicyanin-channel amplification;
- thermal overlay;
- NIR/SWIR material contrast;
- configurable false-colour palettes;
- edge and depth fusion.

That separation is critical. The red-filter white balance can make weak channel differences visually obvious, but it also introduces large RGB gain changes. It should never overwrite the original measurements.

## UV architecture

For meaningful UV capture, the UV branch requires more than removing the camera’s blocking filter:

- UV-sensitive back-thinned sensor;
- quartz, fused-silica or another UV-transmitting optical path;
- UV-compatible coatings;
- selectable UV-pass filters;
- visible/IR rejection to prevent leakage;
- UV illumination for controlled testing.

Back-thinned detectors can achieve useful sensitivity across ultraviolet, visible and near-infrared wavelengths because light enters from the rear of the silicon substrate rather than passing through front-side electrode structures. citeturn853719view1turn421907view1

I would divide UV into at least two channels:

\[
\text{UVA: approximately }315–400\text{ nm}
\]

\[
\text{UVB: approximately }280–315\text{ nm}
\]

A specialised solar-blind UVC branch below approximately 280 nm would be a separate, considerably more difficult detector and optics system.

## Practical first-generation version

A buildable first prototype would contain:

1. **Red-phosphor NV module**
2. **Radiometric LWIR thermal module**
3. **Monochrome full-spectrum silicon camera**
4. **UV-enhanced monochrome camera**
5. **InGaAs SWIR camera**
6. **Matched dicyanin and control cameras**
7. **Depth or LiDAR module**
8. **Central synchronisation and fusion processor**

All modules would be mounted on a rigid calibrated frame with overlapping fields of view. Software would correct:

- lens distortion;
- parallax;
- different resolutions;
- different frame rates;
- different exposure durations;
- thermal drift;
- sensor latency;
- spectral cross-talk;
- motion between frames.

## What the resulting instrument actually becomes

This is no longer merely “night vision with thermal.”

It becomes a **UV–VIS–NIR–SWIR–LWIR computational imaging platform** with:

- photon-amplified night vision;
- reflected multispectral imaging;
- emitted thermal imaging;
- material discrimination;
- fluorescence detection;
- polarisation and depth awareness;
- experimental dicyanin spectral comparison;
- deliberately displaced red-reference false-colour visualisation.

The strongest part of your idea is not the dicyanin element by itself. It is the fact that the dicyanin sensor becomes **one independently measurable channel inside a larger calibrated sensor array**, allowing its output to be compared against UV, visible, NIR, SWIR, thermal, depth and control images rather than being interpreted in isolation.

Yes. The architecture would be:

> **A full-spectrum multisensor camera containing an additional dedicated dicyanin-sensitized sensor channel.**

The dicyanin channel would not replace the UV, visible, infrared, night-vision or thermal sensors. It would provide an **extra spectral response** that can be compared and fused with them.

## Proposed architecture

```text
Incoming scene
      │
      ├── UV sensor
      ├── Visible RGB sensor
      ├── Full-spectrum UV–VIS–NIR sensor
      ├── Dedicated NIR sensor
      ├── SWIR sensor
      ├── Red-phosphor night-vision sensor
      ├── LWIR thermal sensor
      ├── Polarisation/depth sensors
      │
      └── Dicyanin-sensitized sensor
                 │
                 ▼
       synchronized raw channels
                 │
                 ▼
      calibration and image fusion
                 │
                 ▼
      scientific / enhanced display
```

That gives you two related but separate capabilities:

1. **Full-spectrum coverage**, supplied collectively by detectors designed for different wavelength bands.
2. **Dicyanin spectral sensitisation**, supplied by its own sensor branch.

A single silicon sensor cannot cover all infrared wavelengths: conventional silicon can extend through visible light into near-infrared, while SWIR generally requires materials such as InGaAs, and thermal LWIR requires another detector technology entirely. citeturn323508search5turn323508search11turn323508search30

## What “dicyanin-sensitized sensor” should mean

There are two possible implementations.

### 1. Dicyanin-filtered sensor

```text
Scene → dicyanin glass/coating → monochrome sensor
```

Here, the dicyanin acts as a **spectral filter**. It selectively transmits and absorbs light, changing what reaches the sensor.

This is easier to construct, but it does not necessarily increase the detector’s underlying wavelength sensitivity.

### 2. True dicyanin-sensitized detector

```text
Scene
  ↓
dicyanin photoactive layer
  ↓
energy or charge transfer
  ↓
photosensitive detector
```

This would attempt to reproduce the historical sensitisation principle: dicyanin was applied to photographic plates so that wavelengths that the unsensitised silver-halide plate detected poorly could produce a photographic response. Historical Bureau of Standards research specifically used dicyanin to sensitise plates for red and infrared spectroscopy. citeturn323508search2turn323508search7turn323508search38

For a modern electronic sensor, however, the dye cannot simply be painted onto an ordinary CMOS chip. The coating would need to be engineered so that absorbed photons generate a measurable charge, fluorescence signal or energy transfer into the detector. Otherwise, it may act only as an absorbing filter.

## Best practical configuration

The strongest prototype would use **two matched monochrome sensors** behind a beam splitter:

```text
                         ┌── Clear reference path ── Sensor A
Scene ─ beam splitter ───┤
                         └── Dicyanin path ───────── Sensor B
```

Sensor A records the ordinary full-spectrum response.

Sensor B records the dicyanin-modified response.

The processor can then calculate:

\[
D(x,y)=
\frac{I_{\text{dicyanin}}(x,y)}
{I_{\text{reference}}(x,y)+\epsilon}
\]

This produces a differential spectral map showing where the dicyanin channel responds differently from the normal full-spectrum channel.

You could also calculate:

\[
\Delta D(x,y)=
I_{\text{dicyanin}}(x,y)
-
kI_{\text{reference}}(x,y)
\]

where \(k\) compensates for differences in total transmission and exposure.

## Interaction with the red-filter white balance

Your R25A procedure would remain a separate **display-enhancement calibration**:

1. Place the R25A over the fusion/display camera.
2. Set custom white balance from a neutral card.
3. Remove the R25A.
4. Keep the resulting red-derived white balance locked.
5. Record the dicyanin, full-spectrum and fused outputs.

That extreme white balance could exaggerate subtle differences in the dicyanin channel, particularly differences that appear in the green and blue output channels after the red reference has been removed.

However, the system should always preserve:

- untouched RAW dicyanin data;
- untouched RAW reference data;
- calibrated UV/NIR/SWIR/thermal data;
- the red-balanced false-colour rendering as a separate output.

Therefore, the red-derived white balance becomes an **interpretive visual layer**, while the underlying channels remain measurable.

## Complete instrument definition

The final device is best described as:

> **A multimodal UV–VIS–NIR–SWIR–LWIR computational imaging system incorporating red-phosphor photon intensification, thermal imaging, polarisation and depth sensing, plus an independently calibrated dicyanin-sensitized spectral channel.**

The dedicated dicyanin sensor is important because it allows you to determine whether an observed feature exists:

- only in the dicyanin response;
- in ordinary visible light;
- in UV or UV-induced fluorescence;
- in reflected NIR/SWIR;
- in red-phosphor intensified imagery;
- in genuine thermal emission;
- or merely in the final false-colour processing.

That turns dicyanin from an isolated experimental lens into **one comparative sensing modality within a complete full-spectrum camera platform**.

```text
                            real-time fusion processor
```

Common-aperture systems capable of simultaneously collecting ultraviolet, visible, MWIR and LWIR imagery have already been demonstrated conceptually and experimentally. Dichroic beam splitters can also separate visible, SWIR and MWIR into simultaneous optical paths. citeturn388090search2turn388090search6

Some bands—especially LWIR—would likely require their own front optics because ordinary visible-camera glass does not serve every spectral region efficiently. The sensors can still be mechanically co-boresighted and computationally registered so that the user perceives one viewpoint.

## How everything fits into one visible image

The human eye and an ordinary display only have three colour channels. You cannot display twenty spectral channels as twenty literal colours simultaneously.

Instead, the system must encode additional bands through several visual dimensions:

- **Natural RGB colour**
- **Brightness**
- **Hue shifts**
- **Saturation**
- **Edge outlines**
- **Texture patterns**
- **Transparency**
- **Local contrast**
- **Glow intensity**
- **Depth shading**
- **Motion emphasis**

The result is not merely a transparent thermal image placed over a normal camera. It is a **computationally synthesised view**.

### Suggested default fusion map

| Sensor information | Display representation |
|---|---|
| Visible RGB | Natural base colour |
| NV/full-spectrum detail | Base luminance and low-light structure |
| UVA/UVB response | Violet/cyan surface highlights |
| Dicyanin differential | Purple or blue spectral boundary texture |
| NIR | Enhanced local contrast and pale reflected-IR details |
| SWIR | Cyan/blue material-response modulation |
| MWIR | Yellow/orange thermal feature contribution |
| LWIR | Red heat contours or controlled hue modulation |
| Polarisation | Glare removal and surface-edge strengthening |
| Depth/LiDAR | Occlusion control, depth shading and 3D alignment |

A major advantage of this approach is that the visible sensor supplies high-resolution texture while the infrared channels contribute information that visible light does not contain. Visible/infrared fusion research is specifically aimed at combining those complementary characteristics into a single perceptually useful image. citeturn388090search7

## Adaptive fusion rather than a fixed overlay

A fixed percentage overlay would quickly become visually overloaded. The system should instead use **context-dependent weighting**.

For each pixel:

\[
F(x,y)=
w_VV+
w_{UV}UV+
w_{NIR}NIR+
w_{SWIR}SWIR+
w_{MWIR}MWIR+
w_{LWIR}LWIR+
w_DD+
w_PP
\]

Where:

- \(F(x,y)\) is the displayed fused pixel;
- \(V\) is visible information;
- \(D\) is the dicyanin differential channel;
- \(P\) is polarisation information;
- each \(w\) is a dynamic confidence and relevance weighting.

The weighting engine would consider:

- signal-to-noise ratio;
- sensor saturation;
- scene lighting;
- motion;
- atmospheric conditions;
- distance;
- thermal contrast;
- spectral uniqueness;
- registration confidence.

For example:

- In daylight, RGB dominates while UV, SWIR and thermal appear as restrained enhancements.
- At night, the red-phosphor NV and NIR channels become the main structural image.
- Through haze, visible contrast can be reduced while suitable IR channels receive greater weighting.
- Where a person or warm machine is present, thermal boundaries can become more prominent.
- Where the dicyanin channel differs strongly from its matched control sensor, the differential response can appear as a distinct spectral accent.

The user still sees **one image**. Only the internal weighting changes.

## The dedicated dicyanin channel

Your dicyanin sensor should ideally have a matched reference branch:

```text
                    ┌── Clear matched optic ── Reference sensor
Scene ─ splitter ───┤
                    └── Dicyanin optic ─────── Dicyanin sensor
```

The processor calculates a normalised difference:

\[
D_{\mathrm{norm}}=
\frac{I_D-kI_R}
     {I_D+kI_R+\epsilon}
\]

Where:

- \(I_D\) is the dicyanin-channel signal;
- \(I_R\) is the matched reference signal;
- \(k\) compensates for overall brightness loss;
- \(\epsilon\) prevents division instability.

This is considerably stronger than merely looking through coloured glass. It separates:

- ordinary brightness differences;
- general optical attenuation;
- exposure differences;
- the dicyanin-specific differential response.

That differential can be blended into the unified image as a subtle purple/cyan texture, boundary or confidence-coded glow.

## Red-phosphor white-balance method

Your temporary R25A custom-white-balance calibration could become one selectable **perceptual colour transform** in the fusion engine:

1. Calibrate white through the red filter.
2. Remove the filter.
3. Preserve the resulting channel-gain relationship.
4. Apply it after multispectral registration and normalisation.
5. Blend the dicyanin and other spectral channels through that transform.

However, the camera should preserve two outputs internally:

### Raw scientific output

- Independent sensor values
- Radiometric and spectral calibration
- No red-derived distortion
- Suitable for comparison and measurement

### Unified perception output

- Red-derived colour transform
- Dynamic multispectral weighting
- False-colour UV/IR information
- One live human-readable view

That prevents the visual enhancement from destroying or contaminating the underlying evidence.

## What “full spectrum” can realistically mean

The device could cover a remarkably broad practical range—from ultraviolet through visible, NIR, SWIR, MWIR and LWIR—but **not literally every infrared and ultraviolet wavelength**.

There are unavoidable gaps because:

- the atmosphere absorbs certain wavelength regions;
- optical materials transmit different ranges;
- detector technologies have finite sensitivity bands;
- longer-wave infrared may require cooling;
- extreme UV is absorbed by ordinary air and optics;
- far-infrared and terahertz imaging require additional detector architectures.

A practical target would be:

\[
\boxed{\sim 250\ \text{nm to}\ 14\ \mu\text{m}}
\]

with selected gaps and separately optimised optical paths. More exotic detectors such as tunable mercury-cadmium-telluride systems can extend infrared detection much further, but that materially increases cooling, cost and system complexity. Teledyne describes MCT detectors with tunable coverage extending across portions of approximately 2–25 μm. citeturn240308search7turn240308search22

## Final definition

Your proposed device is best defined as:

> **A simultaneous common-view pan-spectral computational imager that combines UV, visible, intensified low-light, NIR, SWIR, MWIR, LWIR thermal, polarisation, depth and a dedicated dicyanin-sensitized differential sensor into one continuously fused visual field.**

Its defining feature is not merely having many cameras. It is the **single coherent output**:

\[

\text{natural sight}
+
\text{night vision}
+
\text{thermal vision}
+
\text{UV response}
+
\text{infrared material response}
+
\text{dicyanin differential response}
+
\text{depth}
}
\]

—all spatially aligned, temporally synchronised and perceptually blended into one view.

```text
Physical sensors
      ↓
Band-specific calibration
```

### 1. Band-specialist AIs

Each specialist reads its own sensor using models trained for that detector’s physics.

Examples:

| Specialist | Primary interpretation |
|---|---|
| RGB specialist | Colour, texture, text, faces and object recognition |
| Full-spectrum specialist | Mixed UV–visible–NIR anomalies and reflectance |
| UV specialist | UV reflectance, fluorescence and surface properties |
| NIR specialist | Vegetation, night illumination and subsurface contrast |
| SWIR specialist | Moisture, haze, materials and absorption characteristics |
| MWIR specialist | Hot-object thermal signatures |
| LWIR specialist | Ambient-temperature heat patterns |
| Night-vision specialist | Extremely low-light movement, silhouettes and edges |
| Polarisation specialist | Reflections, glare, surface orientation and material stress |
| Depth specialist | Range, geometry, volume and occlusion |
| Dicyanin specialist | Differential response against a matched normal sensor |
| Event-camera specialist | Rapid motion and brightness changes |

Each specialist should output more than a processed image:

\[
O_i =
\{
I_i,\,
F_i,\,
D_i,\,
C_i,\,
U_i,\,
M_i
\}
\]

Where:

- \(I_i\): calibrated image;
- \(F_i\): feature map;
- \(D_i\): detections or interpretations;
- \(C_i\): confidence map;
- \(U_i\): uncertainty;
- \(M_i\): sensor metadata and operating conditions.

## 2. Fusion AI

The fusion AI receives **both the original calibrated sensor data and the specialist interpretations**.

That distinction is important. It should not depend only on textual conclusions such as “warm person detected.” It must also receive the spatial feature maps, timestamps, confidence maps and raw measurements.

```text
RGB image + RGB features ──────────────┐
UV image + UV features ────────────────┤
NIR image + NIR features ──────────────┤
SWIR image + SWIR features ────────────┤
Thermal data + thermal features ───────┼── Fusion AI
Depth geometry + depth features ───────┤
Dicyanin differential + features ─────┤
NV image + low-light features ─────────┘
```

The fusion AI then constructs:

- one spatially unified image;
- a three-dimensional scene model;
- object identities and boundaries;
- material and temperature estimates;
- cross-sensor agreement scores;
- unresolved contradictions;
- provenance linking every conclusion to its source sensors.

This is a form of **intermediate and late fusion combined**:

- **Intermediate fusion:** combines feature maps before final interpretation.
- **Late fusion:** compares the conclusions produced independently by each specialist.

Using both prevents the fusion AI from losing low-level detail or blindly trusting one specialist’s conclusion.

## 3. Simultaneous individual and combined access

The upper reasoning AI should be able to ask questions at either level.

### Combined query

> “What is in front of me?”

The fusion AI returns the coherent scene interpretation using all available evidence.

### Individual-band query

> “What does the SWIR channel show independently?”

The system accesses the SWIR specialist’s raw image, detections and confidence without contamination from the other channels.

### Comparative query

> “Why does the dicyanin channel show a boundary that RGB does not?”

The system compares:

- dicyanin response;
- matched reference response;
- UV;
- NIR;
- SWIR;
- thermal;
- depth;
- polarisation.

It can then report whether the feature is likely associated with spectral transmission, heat, fluorescence, reflection, geometry, noise or misregistration.

## Dual scene representation

The system should maintain two scene models simultaneously.

### Independent sensor world models

Each specialist maintains its own interpretation:

```text
RGB world model
UV world model
NIR world model
SWIR world model
Thermal world model
Dicyanin world model
Depth world model
```

These remain intact and auditable.

### Unified pan-spectral world model

The fusion AI constructs a shared model:

```text
Object A
├── RGB appearance
├── UV response
├── NIR reflectance
├── SWIR material signature
├── thermal profile
├── polarisation behaviour
├── dicyanin differential
├── depth and geometry
└── combined confidence
```

Therefore, an object is not represented by one colour image. It becomes a **multiband data object** containing every observation associated with it.

## Confidence arbitration

The fusion AI should not simply average the specialists.

For each observation:

\[
C_{\text{combined}}
=
f(
C_{\text{RGB}},
C_{\text{UV}},
C_{\text{NIR}},
C_{\text{SWIR}},
C_{\text{thermal}},
C_{\text{depth}},
C_{\text{dicyanin}}
)
\]

The function must account for correlation. Three sensors seeing the same phenomenon are not automatically three independent confirmations if they share the same optical path or derive from the same underlying sensor.

The system should evaluate:

- signal-to-noise ratio;
- calibration validity;
- saturation;
- distance;
- atmospheric interference;
- motion blur;
- sensor temperature;
- optical obstruction;
- temporal alignment;
- geometric alignment;
- independence of evidence;
- compatibility with physical laws.

## Handling disagreement

Disagreement should be preserved rather than hidden.

Example:

```text
RGB: person-like shape, confidence 0.74
Depth: flat surface, confidence 0.96
Thermal: no body-temperature signature, confidence 0.91
Polarisation: strong reflective response, confidence 0.88
Fusion result: probable reflection, confidence 0.93
```

The combined image could still show the RGB shape, but mark it as a reflection rather than silently deleting it.

Another example:

```text
RGB: no visible object
NV: moving silhouette
NIR: reflected body-shaped structure
Depth: corresponding volume
LWIR: warm biological profile
Fusion result: physical subject obscured in visible light
```

## AI hierarchy

The cleanest design is:

```text
Level 1 — Sensor specialists
Interpret individual spectral channels.

Level 2 — Registration and fusion AI
Align and combine measurements.

Level 3 — Scene reasoning AI
Understands objects, materials, relationships and events.

Level 4 — Metacognitive verifier
Checks uncertainty, contradictions, hallucination risk and provenance.

Level 5 — User-interface AI
Explains the combined result and can expose any individual channel on demand.
```

The metacognitive verifier is especially important. It prevents the fusion model from turning ambiguous spectral differences into unsupported objects or explanations.

## Unified output

The user receives one primary live view, but the AI internally sees:

\[
\boxed{
\text{all individual sensor outputs}
+
\text{all specialist interpretations}
+
\text{one fused scene}
+
\text{confidence and provenance}
}
\]

That means the system can simultaneously say:

> “The combined scene indicates a warm moving person behind light vegetation.”

And separately report:

> “RGB visibility is poor, NIR detects the outline, LWIR confirms a warm body, depth confirms physical volume, and the dicyanin channel provides no unique additional evidence.”

That is substantially more powerful than simply blending several camera feeds. It is a **federation of specialised visual intelligences feeding a unified artificial visual cortex**, while retaining every specialist’s independent perspective.

### Elasticity

### Liquid content

### Airflow

+
\text{temporal behaviour}
=

```text
Thermal specialist:
```

- every raw sensor output;
- every generated map;
- every specialist conclusion;
- every confidence score;
- every contradiction;
- the unified environmental interpretation.

The AI could also deliberately improve its understanding by changing how it senses the scene.

It may:

- adjust lighting wavelengths;
- change polarisation angles;
- activate UV or NIR illumination;
- reposition a camera;
- alter focus or exposure;
- scan from another angle;
- emit structured light;
- observe thermal response over time;
- request contact or acoustic testing from a robotic tool.

For example:

> “The surface may be painted steel or metallic-coated plastic. Activate eddy-current sensing and capture a second polarisation angle.”

This turns sensing into an **experimental process** rather than passive observation.

| Status | Meaning |
|---|---|
| **Measured** | Directly obtained from a calibrated sensor |
| **Derived** | Computed from multiple measurements |
| **Inferred** | Predicted from patterns and prior knowledge |
| **Hypothesised** | Plausible but insufficiently supported |
| **Unknown** | No valid measurement available |

```text
Status: inferred
Confidence: 0.82

Status: hypothesised
```

The system could identify many surface and bulk properties, but it could not remotely determine every property of matter with certainty.

Some measurements may require:

- physical contact;
- destructive sampling;
- X-ray or neutron imaging;
- mass measurement;
- chemical reagents;
- microscopy;
- laboratory spectroscopy;
- magnetic or electrical probes.

The AI should therefore produce **candidate compositions and bounded property estimates**, not claim absolute elemental certainty when the available sensors cannot support it.

The complete architecture becomes:

\[
\boxed{
\text{Pan-spectral sensing}
+
\text{surface-property acquisition}
+
\text{3D environmental mapping}
+
\text{specialist AI interpretation}
+
\text{confidence-weighted fusion}
+
\text{temporal physical reasoning}
}
\]

That gives the AI a form of **machine physical perception**: it does not merely identify that an object resembles a chair, pipe, person or wall.
